learning_goals: Explain what an LLM is and its limits
Define RAG and each part of the name
Describe the three steps of RAG in order
Identify benefits and a key limitation of RAG

analogy.story: An open‑book exam in school. The student first finds the right page in the textbook, then writes the answer using that page.
analogy.mapping: Finding the page = retrieval. Writing the answer = generation.

worked_example.setting: Riya, a college student in Pune, uses a chatbot on her college website.
worked_example.question: What is the last date to apply for the scholarship?
documents: The scholarship amount is ₹10,000 per year.
worked_example.answer_with_rag: The last date to apply is 31 March 2025.

sections.heading: What You Will Learn
sections.goal: List the skills you will gain in this lesson.
points: Explain what an LLM is and its limits (F1‑F4)
Define RAG and each word in the name (F5)
Describe the three RAG steps in order (F8)
Name benefits and a key limitation of RAG (F11‑F12)

sections.heading: Before We Start: Some Basic Ideas
sections.goal: Understand what an LLM is and its limits.
points: LLM is a model trained on huge text (F1)
LLM knowledge stops at a cutoff date (F2)
LLM does not know private data (F3)
LLM can hallucinate, giving confident wrong answers (F4)

sections.heading: What Is RAG?
sections.goal: Define RAG and each word in the name.
points: RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation (F5)
Retrieval = finding relevant information (F5)
Augmented = adding that information to the prompt (F5)
Generation = LLM writes the answer (F5)
RAG does not retrain the model (F9)

sections.heading: Why Does RAG Matter?
sections.goal: Explain the benefits of using RAG.
points: Uses fresh and private data (F11)
Reduces hallucinations (F11)
Shows sources for answers (F11)
Cheaper than retraining the model (F11)
Easy to update knowledge by changing documents (F11)

sections.heading: How Does RAG Work?
sections.goal: Describe preparation and the three question‑time steps.
points: Preparation: split documents into chunks, turn each chunk into an embedding (list of numbers) using an embedding model, store in a vector database (F7)
Step 1 Retrieve: turn the question into an embedding, find top‑k similar chunks with semantic search (F8)
Step 2 Augment: put retrieved chunks into the prompt with an instruction (F8)
Step 3 Generate: LLM writes the answer from the prompt (F8)
Model weights stay unchanged (F9)
Fine‑tuning changes weights and is slower (F10)

sections.heading: Example: College Scholarship Chatbot
sections.goal: Show a concrete RAG flow with a real question.
points: User asks the scholarship deadline question
System retrieves the correct snippet from the knowledge base
Answer is built using the retrieved text
Without RAG the LLM gives an outdated date

sections.heading: Key Words to Remember
sections.goal: List important terms with simple definitions.
points: LLM – large language model (F1)
Knowledge cutoff – date after which model knows nothing (F2)
Hallucination – confident wrong answer (F4)
RAG – Retrieval-Augmented Generation (F5)
Chunk – small piece of a document (F7)
Embedding – list of numbers that captures meaning (F7)
Vector database – searchable store of embeddings (F7)
Semantic search – search by meaning not keywords (F8)
Top‑k – number of top chunks used (F8)
Context window – max text the prompt can hold (F12)
Fine‑tuning – further training that changes model weights (F10)

sections.heading: Quick Check
sections.goal: Test understanding with a few questions.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.goal: Recap the main ideas of the lesson.
points: LLM has limits: cutoff, no private data, hallucinations
RAG adds external information before answering
Three steps: retrieve, augment, generate
No retraining needed; just update documents
Answer quality depends on retrieval quality

quiz.q: Which step comes first when a user asks a question in RAG?
Does RAG change the model's weights?
quiz.a: No, RAG does not retrain or change the model.

quiz.q: What is one limitation of RAG?
quiz.a: The answer is only as good as the retrieved chunks; bad retrieval leads to wrong answers.

quiz.q: Why is RAG cheaper than fine‑tuning?
quiz.a: RAG only updates documents, not the model, so no extra training cost.
